query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys (HEAs), resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by the formation of a dynamic, self-healing, compositionally complex oxide passivation layer. Under mechanical stress, localized atomic rearrangements promote segregation of corrosion‐resistant elements, which then form a protective oxide that simultaneously reduces material loss from wear and impedes corrosive attack.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized, as-synthesized high-entropy alloy with a uniform microstructure (e.g., a finely polished surface showing no pre-existing oxide layers).
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA to a coupled mechanical wear test (such as a pin-on-disk sliding test) while immersing it in a corrosive environment (e.g., a chloride-rich aqueous solution) under controlled temperature conditions.
generation.conditions: Test conditions should mimic a harsh corrosive mechanical environment: moderate to high mechanical loads, controlled sliding speeds, elevated temperatures, and aggressive electrolyte conditions (e.g., high chloride concentration) that are severe enough to induce both wear and corrosion but still allow the formation of surface oxides.
generation.structural_mediator: The self-forming, self-healing oxide/hydroxide passivation layer enriched in corrosion-resistant elements (e.g., Cr, Al, Mo, depending on the HEA composition) which arises from wear-induced elemental segregation.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear promotes local plastic deformation and atomic diffusion, leading to elemental segregation at exposed surfaces. This enrichment facilitates the rapid formation of a complex oxide layer that is mechanically robust (resisting further wear) and chemically inert (hindering corrosive attack).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a matched baseline (either a conventional alloy or a treated HEA sample prevented from forming the dynamic oxide), the HEA under simultaneous wear and corrosion will exhibit a lower cumulative degradation: reduced wear volume loss, fewer and shallower corrosion pits, and an overall smaller synergistic degradation effect due to the protective passivation layer.
generation.baseline: A comparable conventional alloy or an HEA sample modified (e.g., via a surface treatment) to inhibit the formation of the dynamic oxide layer, tested under identical mechanical and corrosive conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold under conditions where both the rate of oxide formation and its adhesion are sustained—typically under moderate to high, but not extreme, wear and corrosion stresses. At extreme conditions (such as very high temperatures or excessively aggressive environments), the oxide layer may break down or fail to reform rapidly, and the prediction may not hold.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of oxide formation, its compositional specifics, and the threshold conditions (mechanical and chemical) for sustaining the protective effect remain uncertain and likely vary with alloy composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the target high-entropy alloy and another set of a baseline alloy (or an HEA modified to disrupt oxide formation). Subject both sets to simultaneous wear (using a pin-on-disk apparatus) and immersion in a high chloride concentration solution at an elevated temperature over a fixed number of cycles. Use surface analysis techniques to characterize oxide layer formation and measure the extent of wear and corrosion.
measurements: Corrosion pit density and depth using microscopic analysis
Oxide layer thickness and composition via XPS and TEM
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to assess surface passivation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA does not show a distinctly thicker or compositionally enriched self-healing oxide layer compared to the baseline, or if its wear and corrosion rates are statistically similar to (or worse than) those of the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.
